title: "Overview of Ecosystem Service: Water Supply"

Water supply is built one component at a time. Hydropower direct use is computed and is what
`water_supply_gep` currently carries, with its treatment of negative rents still open. The agricultural and municipal components are reported
beside it as separate columns. The municipal value, `water_use_domestic_gep`, is the authors'
final table. The price convention recorded in `es_config.csv`, `resource rent (CWoN 2024)`,
describes the hydropower component. The municipal component is a replacement cost, described
below. The base year is 2019.

## Hydropower

### Quantity and price

The hydropower valuation has no separate quantity and price step. CWoN 2024 publishes a
capitalised hydropower wealth per country, and the annual rent that wealth implies is what the
account wants.

### Valuation

`annuity_factor` is the present value of one dollar a year over the CWoN horizon,

$$
A = \sum_{t=1}^{100} \frac{1}{(1+r)^t}, \qquad r = 0.04
$$

and `hydropower_rent_from_wealth` divides each country's `YR2019` wealth by it. Countries without
wealth stay NaN, because no data is not zero rent.

This wealth-based value is what the account reports while the treatment of negative rents is
undecided. Beside it, `hydropower_rent_from_revenue_and_cost` computes the authors' 2019 resource
rent directly: revenues (column W) minus total costs (column Y) of the hydropower rows of the
World Bank's CWoN 2024 hydropower valuation workbook, sheet `Database`, in nominal USD (equal to
2019 USD for 2019). The sign is kept in `hydropower_rent_signed_usd`, and
`hydropower_rent_status` says positive, negative, zero or missing. Countries are keyed by the
CWoN wealth table's own names and codes, with three newer World Bank names (Czechia, North
Macedonia, Türkiye) mapped to that table's earlier ones. An earlier direct-use script on the
drive, price times quantity from EIA and World Bank series dated November 2024, is superseded and
is not ported.

### Source

The write-up is `Hydropower_Provision.docx` in the shared folder of current write-ups (version of
27 October 2026). It values the rent as max(0, rent), with no separate λ because the rent already
nets costs out of price times quantity. The registered author code is `lifengren95/gep_hydropower`
at `7f45eb4`. It imports a prepared CWoN rent table in 2019 USD. The authors confirmed on 30
October that the table is the valuation workbook's 2019 revenues minus total costs, computed in
Excel, with no script. The workbook (rev4, sha256 `e7c6e7f6…`) was provided by World Bank staff,
is not in the public reproducibility package and is not to be redistributed. It is staged only
where authorised and checked against its recorded hash. Without it the run proceeds and the
revenue-minus-cost columns are missing, with status "workbook not staged".

### Coverage

`hydropower_gep` carries 107 positive values, totalling \$146,075,770,382.38, 5 zeros where the
CWoN wealth is zero, and 138 missing countries with no wealth figure.
The workbook gives 112 countries a 2019 rent: 95 positive, \$144,680,445,647.89, and 17 negative,
−\$1,518,729,566.45. `hydropower_gep_reference_variant` is the positive rents with the rest left
missing, the convention of the authors' output. It exists for comparison and is not the reported
value. It equals the authors' 95 rents in every country, within \$1 because their file stores whole
dollars, with the same 17 left blank. The wealth-based value equals the workbook's rent in the 95
positive countries. `water_supply_gep` is `hydropower_gep`.

## Water use

### Quantity and price

Withdrawal volumes in cubic metres per sector come from the withdrawal table. The price is the
AQUASTAT SDG 6.4.1 water-use efficiency series in US dollars per cubic metre, one series per
sector.

### Valuation

`clean_aquastat_water_efficiency` is script 01 of the drive's R calculation. It keeps the US$/m3 rows of
the four SDG 6.4.1 series and pivots them wide by country and year.

`water_use_gep_by_country_year` is script 02. It applies three country renames onto the withdrawal
table's spellings, fills iso codes for the names its country map does not carry, drops the
regional aggregate rows, merges the two tables, restricts to the survey years, and multiplies
efficiency by withdrawal per sector to give `gep_water_agricultural`, `gep_water_industrial` and
`gep_water_municipal`.

`water_use_components_from_chain` takes the latest survey year per country and keys it to r250 by
exact country-name match, first on `iso3_r250_name` and then on `name_long`. A calculation country with
no match keeps an empty iso3, so a name drift is visible instead of dropped.

Both of the R calculation's own outputs replicate. The cleaned efficiency table matches bit-exactly. The
country-year GEP table matches to the anchor CSV's own 15-significant-digit rounding, maximum
relative difference 3e-15.

## Agricultural water

### Quantity and price

The quantity side is Shunkei's crop-level water accounting: per CropGBWater crop, country and
water source, a lambda coefficient in [0, 1], the Ky-weighted mean of growth-stage
water-satisfaction ratios, for rainfed green water, irrigated green water and irrigated blue
water, with a VMR pair reported beside the green components, never netted against them. The
price side is the value of the crop: lambda times a rainfed/irrigated value basis gives the
water-attributable share of that value.

Lambda is biophysical, a Ky-weighted mean of growth-stage water-satisfaction ratios, not a share
of water volume or of value. Multiplying it by a monetary value attributes that value to water
in proportion, which is an assumption of the method, not a measured water rent. The author
first applied it to crop value added (gross production value times θ, the
agricultural value-added share) and confirmed on 28 October 2026 that the monetary base is now
commercial-agriculture GEP, the crop rent this account uses.

### Valuation

`agriculture_basis_from_crop_values` rebuilds the author's value preparation (the author's Code/1-4) on
the account's own crop values. FAOSTAT items map to CropGBWater crops through the author's
correspondence, many-to-one items sum, the two shared items (Wheat and Millet) allocate by the author's
SPAM production-quantity weights within country and item, and SPAM rainfed/irrigated shares
split each crop-country value into `basis_rain` and `basis_irr`, with the author's own split-status
labels where the SPAM row is absent or zero. One departure is documented in the docstring: an
all-missing group stays missing instead of the author's na.rm zero, because the account's table carries
genuine gaps and a fabricated zero would read as measured.

`agriculture_gep_from_lambda` is the author's final stage (Code/5): the three lambda-times-basis
products, their VMR pair, and `GEP_total` as the rowwise sum over the three components with
missing treated as zero, replicated from the author with partial totals included.
`aggregate_agriculture_gep_to_country` is the author's sum-if-any country aggregation.

The replication and the account run are not the same calculation. The test suite feeds the two
functions the author's own theta x GPV 2020 basis in thousand current US$ and reproduces the author's
September 21 crop-country and country results within measured float-reordering noise. The
`agriculture_water` task instead feeds the account's 2019 commercial crop-provision values in
current USD, with the CWoN rental rate already applied, so no theta and no rental
re-application, split rainfed/irrigated by the author's SPAM shares. The 2019 substitution is the
account's decision, not the author's output. The author's upstream lambda, SPAM, crop-mapping and theta
derivations are taken as given, and matching the author's final-stage outputs proves fidelity, not
correctness.

2019 is the monetary year only. The physical inputs carry their own vintages. The SPAM shares
are SPAM 2020 v2r2 (the author's Code/1-3, the Harvard Dataverse release), and lambda is built on a
representative 365-day daily ET0 profile averaged over 2018-2022 (the author's Code/3).

Under the meeting convention this value is an intermediate contribution: the basis is the
crop-provision GEP itself, so the agricultural-water figure is the water-attributable share of
value already counted in crop provision. It is reported for attribution and is never added to a
GEP total beside crop provision. That classification keeps water from being counted twice. It
does not make the value a water-only rent: the crop rent prices land and water together, so the
figure is the water-attributable part of a joint rent.

Coverage is disclosed rather than repaired. Items with no correspondence row stay out of the
basis and are written to `agriculture_unmapped_items.csv`. Rice is the largest. Crop-country
values whose SPAM row is absent or zero stay unsplit and carry their status. Split basis rows
with no lambda coefficients are written to `agriculture_missing_coefficients.csv`, and
`agriculture_coverage.csv` summarizes the value at each stage.

## Municipal water

The published municipal value is the authors' final table: their `Results/dr02` output at
commit `f94e33a4` of `lifengren95/gep_domestic_water_supply`. They confirmed it as final. It
matches column N of the group's 2026_10_01 values sheet within the sheet's reported precision:
each country agrees within 4.4e-9 relative, and the totals are $9,231,821,271.88 in the table
against $9,231,821,270.68 in the sheet. The library imports it rather than recomputing it, and
it has not rerun the authors' city optimisation. `municipal_gep_by_country` checks the labels, refuses an unknown or repeated
label and a negative value, and leaves a country without a value missing.

### Quantity and price

Each city is a GHSL 2025 urban centre of at least 50,000 people. Its demand is its population
times the country's 2019 AQUASTAT municipal withdrawal per person. Without a 2019 AQUASTAT
rate the model cannot estimate a territory's demand, so it cannot value it, and such
territories are missing, not zero. Sixteen territories with 52 urban centres are in that
position, the largest being Taiwan (21), Hong Kong (6) and Kosovo (6). The model values
municipal demand only: industrial withdrawals, which the earlier construction counted, are not
valued in this row. The authors then cost the
cheapest way to meet that demand from nearby rivers, lakes and reservoirs (RiverATLAS and
LakeATLAS, within 100 km, 30% of mean flow, intakes in protected areas excluded) and from
groundwater (SuperWell).

- Pipeline costs come from EPA cost curves, using FABDEM elevations.
- Pumping is priced at World Bank 2019 electricity prices.
- Infrastructure is annualised at a 2% discount rate.

### Valuation

$$
\text{GEP}_i = C_i^{\text{replacement}} - C_i^{\text{baseline}}
$$

per city. The replacement problem removes two things and solves again with everything else
unchanged:

- the surface-water sources selected in the baseline, together with the candidates recorded as
  drawing on the same flow path,
- groundwater, if the baseline used it.

A city is valued only where both the baseline and the replacement problem are feasible. A city
whose demand cannot be met stays undefined, and the model has no desalination.

The country value sums the valued cities only (the authors'
`Analysis/10_country_municipal_replacement_cost.qmd` aggregates
`y_city_shared_flowpath_replacement_30.csv` and keeps the coverage counts). A country with some
cities unvalued therefore carries a partial total, not the value of all its municipal demand.
The table holds 160 countries and $9,231,821,271.88 in total.

### The earlier construction, kept as a variant

`water_use_domestic_gep_implied_price_variant` is the water-use chain's earlier stand-in: ecosystem-provided
cubic metres (withdrawal net of desalination) times a raw-water price implied by the old
irrigation premium ($0.0852/m³). It is $95.62bn over 183 countries. It is kept for comparison
only and is not the account's figure.

## Inputs

From `es_parameters.csv`, scoped to the `water_supply` service:

- `water_supply_cwon_hydro_wealth_path`, the CWoN `hydro_wealth_cd` table, with a `_source_url`
  row for the World Bank reproducibility archive and a `_source_archive_member` row naming the
  file inside it.
- `water_supply_cwon_hydro_workbook_path` and `water_supply_cwon_hydro_workbook_sha256`, the
  private valuation workbook and its hash, with a `_source` row on where it comes from and that
  it is not to be redistributed.
- `water_use_efficiency_input_path`, the raw AQUASTAT export, with a `_source_url` row for the
  AQUASTAT data API.
- `water_use_withdrawal_path`, the withdrawal table.
- `water_use_agriculture_path` and `water_use_all_sector_path`, the drive's committed per-country
  tables, held as comparison anchors.
- `water_supply_agriculture_lambda_path`, `water_supply_agriculture_spam_path` and
  `water_supply_agriculture_correspondence_path`, the author's pinned processed tables under
  `agriculture/shunkei_e229f881/` in base_data, with a `water_supply_agriculture_source` row
  and a provenance README beside the files.
- `water_supply_municipal_results_path`, the authors' final municipal table under
  `municipal/lifeng_f94e33a4_dr02/` in base_data, with a `water_supply_municipal_results_source`
  row and a provenance README beside the file.
- `water_supply_crop_values_path`, the commercial crop country-item table in USD, blank by
  default: the task falls back to the crop_provision results registry, then to
  `water_supply_crop_values_relative_file` against the project directory. Reading the
  producer's own path removes the copy, not the staleness: the table is only as fresh as the
  last crop_provision run, so the agriculture figure's provenance includes the crop_provision
  run that wrote it, and a crop_provision change requires regenerating that table before this
  service's figure is quoted.

## Outputs

- `hydropower_rent.csv` from the `hydropower_rent` task.
- `aquastat_water_efficiency_cleaned.csv`, `water_use_gep_by_country_year.csv` and
  `water_use_components.csv` from the `water_use_components` task.
- `agriculture_by_country.csv` and `agriculture_by_crop_country.csv` from the
  `agriculture_water` task, with `agriculture_basis.csv`, `agriculture_coverage.csv` and the
  diagnostic tables (unmapped items, missing coefficients, unallocated shared value, unsplit
  statuses) beside them.
- `gep_by_country_base_year.csv` from `gep_calculation`, holding the r250 identifiers and
  attributes, `year`, the hydropower pair, the water-use value-added columns, the municipal value
  `water_use_domestic_gep` (the authors' table) with `water_use_domestic_gep_implied_price_variant`
  beside it, the agriculture component columns (`water_use_agriculture_gep` with its rainfed/irrigated and VMR
  parts, and `water_use_irrigation_gep` now equal to the agriculture component), and
  `water_supply_gep`.

## Method constants

- `water_supply_hydropower_capitalization_rate = 0.04` in `es_parameters`, the rate CWoN
  capitalized their wealth figure with.

  This is not the account's discount rate. The account discounts future benefits at 2 percent,
  with sensitivity at 1 and 3. This rate does the opposite job: CWoN published a *capitalized*
  wealth figure, and hydropower GEP is the annual rent inside it, so the module runs their
  capitalization backwards. Inverting with any other rate returns a rent CWoN never capitalized.
  The consistency gate reports both rates. A review comment proposes 2 percent here, which is
  open (see below).
- `HYDROPOWER_HORIZON_YEARS = 100`, the CWoN capitalisation horizon.
- `HYDROPOWER_GEP_YEAR = 2019`, the wealth column the rent is read from. Current USD equals real
  2019 USD in the 2019 base year, and this is the only variant that covers Venezuela.
- `HYDROPOWER_WORKBOOK_SHEET`, `HYDROPOWER_WORKBOOK_REVENUE` and `HYDROPOWER_WORKBOOK_COST`,
  the workbook's sheet and the headers of columns W and Y, which the code checks sit in those
  columns, and `HYDROPOWER_WORKBOOK_RENAMES`, the three name mappings above.
- `WATER_USE_YEARS = (2000, 2005, 2010, 2015)`, the AQUASTAT survey years the calculation keeps.
- `WATER_USE_EFFICIENCY_SERIES`, `WATER_USE_COUNTRY_RENAMES`, `WATER_USE_ISO_LOOKUP` and
  `WATER_USE_REGIONS_DROPPED`, which reproduce script 02's name surgery verbatim.

## Taken as given

CWoN's own hydropower wealth estimate, and the AQUASTAT efficiency and withdrawal series.

## What is open

Hydropower, two open points:

- Negative rents. The workbook's 2019 rent is negative in 17 countries. The authors' output
  leaves them blank, the write-up floors them at zero, and the wealth-based value the account
  reports gives 12 of them \$1,395,324,734.50 in all, because their CWoN wealth is positive (the
  other 5 have zero wealth and report zero). Which treatment the account uses is undecided, so the
  library keeps the signed rent and does not choose.
- The capitalisation rate. The wealth-based value inverts at CWoN's 4 percent. A review comment
  proposes 2 percent, which is under review.

The drive's per-country water-use tables are not this calculation's outputs and are held as anchors
rather than adopted. The agriculture table equals 1000 times `GEP_total` from the crop-water
valuation whose scripts are now identified and pinned: the Shunkei repository this module
replicates. The all-sector table was computed on a newer AQUASTAT
vintage with the appendix's deflate-to-2015 step, and only 3 of 183 countries reproduce from the
staged inputs, with a median committed to computed-at-2019 ratio of 0.36 over a range of 0 to 1.25.

Script 02's lookup countries keep their AQUASTAT names, so their efficiency and withdrawal rows
share an iso code but never a country name. The merge leaves them as half-rows with no products,
including USA, RUS and TUR. The anchor commits that behaviour and the port reproduces it.

`water_supply_gep` stays the hydropower component alone. How, and whether, the water-use and
agriculture components combine with it is the account's subgroup question, flagged on the deck.

The municipal table is carried, not reproduced: the library has not rerun the authors' city
optimisation. Their write-up still has open review comments, including a λ section and why 2025
population serves the 2019 base year.

The agriculture correspondence is read as an input of the author's pipeline (Code/1-4). No
generating script for it was found in the inspected revision. It covers 28 crops, and the three
inspected coefficient and share tables (`lambda_jr_tbl_CropGBWater.csv`,
`CropGBWater_FAO_Ky_Kc.csv`, `spam_cropgbwater_share.csv`) carry exactly those 28. The account's
crop table carries value on items outside them, rice above all, which therefore cannot enter
the basis with the supplied tables, disclosed in `agriculture_unmapped_items.csv`. Extending the
set needs correspondence rows AND coefficients produced with the author's pipeline. No local
mapping change can do it.
